blocks.en: Radical Discipleship · "Whoever Desires to Come After Me, Let Him Deny Himself" (Matt 16:24)
blocks.es_reference: Discipulado Radical · "Si Alguno Quiere Venir en Pos de Mí, Niéguese a Sí Mismo" (Mat 16:24)

blocks.en: Course Author: Dr. Wayne Cook · Chapala Theological Seminary
blocks.es_reference: Autor del Curso: Dr. Wayne Cook · Seminario Teológico de Chapala

blocks.en: When Jesus said, "No one pours new wine into old wineskins" (Luke 5:37-38), He was introducing a new kind of disciple. The old religious container — the Pharisees' rigid, brittle system — could not hold what He was pouring. Radical discipleship is the new wineskin. It begins not with a new program but with a single, hard sentence: Whoever desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me (Matt 16:24). This unit follows that sentence through three movements: the new wineskin Jesus brought, the cost He named, and the counterfeit the world keeps offering instead.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Jesús dijo, "Nadie echa vino nuevo en odres viejos" (Lucas 5:37-38), estaba introduciendo una nueva clase de discípulo. El viejo contenedor religioso — el sistema rígido y frágil de los fariseos — no podía contener lo que Él estaba vertiendo. El discipulado radical es el odre nuevo. Comienza no con un programa nuevo sino con una sola oración dura: Si alguno quiere venir en pos de Mí, niéguese a sí mismo, y tome su cruz, y sígame (Mat 16:24). Esta unidad sigue esa oración a través de tres movimientos: el odre nuevo que Jesús trajo, el costo que Él nombró, y la falsificación que el mundo sigue ofreciendo en su lugar.

blocks.en: 1. New Wine, New Wineskins
blocks.es_reference: 1. Vino Nuevo, Odres Nuevos

blocks.en: Matthew 9:16-17 (NKJV): "No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for the patch pulls away from the garment, and the tear is made worse. Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins, or else the wineskins break, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined. But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved."
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 9:16-17 (RVG): "Nadie pone remiendo de paño nuevo en vestido viejo; porque tal remiendo tira del vestido, y la rotura se hace peor. Ni echan vino nuevo en odres viejos; de otra manera los odres se rompen, y el vino se derrama, y los odres se pierden; mas echan el vino nuevo en odres nuevos, y lo uno y lo otro se conserva."

blocks.en: The image is from the kitchen, not from a theology classroom. New wine ferments. The sugar in the juice becomes gas, the gas expands, the container has to stretch. A fresh leather wineskin gives a little as the wine breathes, then a little more, then settles when the fermentation finishes. An old wineskin, used up and brittle, has no give left in it. The same pressure that a new skin absorbs splits an old one open. The wine ends up on the floor and the skin ends up in the trash. Jesus' point is not about wine. His point is about people. The disciple He is making is fermenting; the disciple cannot be contained inside an old religious system that has no room left to stretch.
blocks.es_reference: La imagen viene de la cocina, no de un aula de teología. El vino nuevo fermenta. El azúcar en el jugo se vuelve gas, el gas se expande, el contenedor tiene que estirarse. Un odre fresco de cuero cede un poco mientras el vino respira, luego un poco más, luego se asienta cuando la fermentación termina. Un odre viejo, gastado y frágil, no tiene flexibilidad que le quede. La misma presión que un odre nuevo absorbe parte a uno viejo. El vino termina en el piso y el odre termina en la basura. El punto de Jesús no es sobre el vino. Su punto es sobre las personas. El discípulo que Él está haciendo está fermentando; el discípulo no puede ser contenido dentro de un viejo sistema religioso que no tiene espacio para estirarse.

blocks.en: The context in Matthew 9 makes this concrete. The Pharisees were complaining about two things. First, Jesus was eating with tax collectors and sinners instead of with respectable religious people. Second, His disciples were not fasting on the days the Pharisees fasted. Both complaints are about containers. The Pharisees had a fixed shape for what a holy man should look like, and Jesus did not fit it. Rather than asking whether their shape might be wrong, they concluded He must be wrong. That is what an old wineskin does. It does not stretch to receive new wine; it splits, blames the wine, and throws it away.
blocks.es_reference: El contexto de Mateo 9 hace esto concreto. Los fariseos se quejaban de dos cosas. Primero, Jesús comía con recaudadores de impuestos y pecadores en vez de con gente religiosa respetable. Segundo, Sus discípulos no ayunaban en los días que los fariseos ayunaban. Ambas quejas son sobre contenedores. Los fariseos tenían una forma fija de cómo debía verse un hombre santo, y Jesús no encajaba. En vez de preguntar si su forma podría estar equivocada, concluyeron que Él debía estar equivocado. Eso es lo que hace un odre viejo. No se estira para recibir vino nuevo; se parte, culpa al vino, y lo tira.

blocks.en: Mrs. Brown's Milk Jugs: When I was a teenager, my mother was working, cooking, and doing the laundry — sometimes ironing late at night. She hired a lady named Mrs. Brown to do the ironing, and my job was to take the clothes there and pick them up later. Mrs. Brown had some milk jugs filled with colored liquid, with tubes coming from them and leading down into a basin of water. I asked her what they were. She said it was wine inside; when the bubbles stopped coming up through the water, the wine was finished. That is what new wine does — it bubbles and ferments because the sugar in the juice is alive. A rigid container cannot hold that.
blocks.es_reference: Los Frascos de Leche de la Sra. Brown: Cuando yo era adolescente, mi madre estaba trabajando, cocinando, y haciendo la lavandería — a veces planchando hasta tarde por la noche. Contrató a una señora llamada Sra. Brown para que hiciera el planchado, y mi tarea era llevar la ropa allá y recogerla más tarde. La Sra. Brown tenía unos frascos de leche llenos de un líquido coloreado, con tubos saliendo de ellos y bajando a una vasija de agua. Le pregunté qué eran. Dijo que era vino adentro; cuando dejaran de subir burbujas a través del agua, el vino estaba terminado. Eso es lo que hace el vino nuevo — burbujea y fermenta porque el azúcar en el jugo está vivo. Un contenedor rígido no puede contener eso.

blocks.en: Faith in Christ behaves like the wine in those milk jugs. It is alive. It is expansive. It does not sit politely inside whatever religious shape the disciple grew up in. The new wineskin of radical discipleship has to stretch. Stretching is painful — that is the part nobody volunteers for. Many believers reach the first stretch and decide they would rather have an unbroken old skin than a new one full of strange pressure. The wine spills. The skin is intact but empty. This is the most common kind of failure in church history: not heresy but rigidity, not denial but stiffness. The Pharisees were not bad men by the world's standards. They were religious men whose containers could no longer hold what God was pouring.
blocks.es_reference: La fe en Cristo se comporta como el vino en esos frascos de leche. Está viva. Es expansiva. No se sienta cortésmente dentro de cualquier forma religiosa en la que el discípulo creció. El odre nuevo del discipulado radical tiene que estirarse. Estirarse es doloroso — esa es la parte para la que nadie se ofrece voluntariamente. Muchos creyentes alcanzan el primer estiramiento y deciden que prefieren tener un odre viejo intacto que uno nuevo lleno de presión extraña. El vino se derrama. El odre queda intacto pero vacío. Esta es la clase de fracaso más común en la historia de la iglesia: no herejía sino rigidez, no negación sino tiesura. Los fariseos no eran malos hombres según los estándares del mundo. Eran hombres religiosos cuyos contenedores ya no podían sostener lo que Dios estaba vertiendo.

blocks.en: 2. The Cost
blocks.es_reference: 2. El Costo

blocks.en: Matthew 16:24-25 (NKJV): "Then Jesus said to His disciples, 'If anyone desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.'"
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 16:24-25 (RVG): "Entonces Jesús dijo a sus discípulos: Si alguno quiere venir en pos de Mí, niéguese a sí mismo, y tome su cruz, y sígame. Porque cualquiera que quisiere salvar su vida, la perderá; y cualquiera que perdiere su vida por causa de Mí, la hallará."

blocks.en: The cost Jesus names is not abstract. Deny himself — the self is the largest obstacle. Take up his cross — and a cross in the first century was not jewelry; it was the instrument of public, shameful execution. Roman crucifixion was reserved for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals. When Jesus said take up your cross to a Galilean crowd, they understood Him to be talking about literal death and literal disgrace. There was no devotional softness in the image. He was naming the price of becoming His disciple, and the price was everything.
blocks.es_reference: El costo que Jesús nombra no es abstracto. Niéguese a sí mismo — el yo es el obstáculo más grande. Tome su cruz — y una cruz en el primer siglo no era joyería; era el instrumento de ejecución pública y vergonzosa. La crucifixión romana estaba reservada para esclavos, rebeldes, y los criminales más bajos. Cuando Jesús dijo tomad vuestra cruz a una multitud galilea, ellos entendieron que estaba hablando de muerte literal y deshonra literal. No había suavidad devocional en la imagen. Estaba nombrando el precio de volverse Su discípulo, y el precio era todo.

blocks.en: Jesus did not require of His disciples anything He had not already done Himself. Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9). The Lord of glory left the throne. He took a body. He took a stable for a birthplace and a manger for a crib. He had no house during His ministry, and as far as we can tell He had no savings; He had a nice cloak that someone had given Him. He had no horse, and had to borrow a colt for His final entrance into Jerusalem. He had no grave, but had to borrow one when He died — though He did return it three days later, only slightly used. Every choice He made was a downward step. Luke records the turning point in His ministry in a single sentence: He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). He knew what was waiting there. He went anyway.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús no requirió de Sus discípulos nada que Él mismo no hubiera hecho. Aunque era rico, por amor a vosotros se hizo pobre, para que vosotros con Su pobreza fueseis enriquecidos (2 Cor 8:9). El Señor de gloria dejó el trono. Tomó un cuerpo. Tomó un establo por lugar de nacimiento y un pesebre por cuna. No tuvo casa durante Su ministerio, y hasta donde podemos decir no tuvo ahorros; tenía un buen manto que alguien le había dado. No tuvo caballo, y tuvo que pedir prestado un pollino para Su entrada final a Jerusalén. No tuvo tumba, pero tuvo que pedir prestada una cuando murió — aunque la devolvió tres días después, solo ligeramente usada. Cada decisión que tomó fue un paso hacia abajo. Lucas registra el punto de giro en Su ministerio en una sola oración: afirmó Su rostro para ir a Jerusalén (Lucas 9:51). Sabía lo que esperaba allí. Fue de todos modos.

blocks.en: The disciples followed the same pattern, slowly at first and then completely. They sacrificed their jobs at the start — nets dropped on the beach, a tax table abandoned in mid-collection. They sacrificed their reputations next, walking with a teacher the religious authorities openly hated. By the end of the first century, most of them had sacrificed their lives. James was beheaded (Acts 12:2); church tradition, well-attested though not itself Scripture, holds that Peter was crucified and Andrew and Thomas died as martyrs as well, Thomas as far away as India; only John lived to old age, and he lived it in exile on Patmos. The standard for radical commitment did not change between Jesus and the apostles. Whoever wants to come after Me still means deny self, take up cross, follow.
blocks.es_reference: Los discípulos siguieron el mismo patrón, lentamente al principio y luego completamente. Sacrificaron sus trabajos al inicio — redes dejadas en la playa, una mesa de impuestos abandonada en medio de la recaudación. Sacrificaron sus reputaciones después, caminando con un maestro que las autoridades religiosas odiaban abiertamente. Para el final del primer siglo, la mayoría había sacrificado sus vidas. Jacobo fue decapitado (Hechos 12:2); la tradición de la iglesia, bien atestiguada aunque no es Escritura misma, sostiene que Pedro fue crucificado y que Andrés y Tomás también murieron como mártires, Tomás tan lejos como India; solo Juan vivió hasta la vejez, y la vivió en exilio en Patmos. El estándar para el compromiso radical no cambió entre Jesús y los apóstoles. Si alguno quiere venir en pos de Mí aún significa negarse a sí mismo, tomar la cruz, seguir.

blocks.en: And the same standard reaches farther back. Abraham was willing to lay his only son on the altar. Peter and the apostles stood before the Sanhedrin and said we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), knowing exactly what the consequences would be. Across the testaments, the disciple's mark is the same: there is something more valuable to him than his own life, and he knows what it is. The cost is named in advance, accepted in advance, and paid out across the years one obedience at a time.
blocks.es_reference: Y el mismo estándar alcanza más atrás. Abraham estuvo dispuesto a poner a su único hijo en el altar. Pedro y los apóstoles se pararon ante el Sanedrín y dijeron es necesario obedecer a Dios antes que a los hombres (Hch 5:29), sabiendo exactamente cuáles serían las consecuencias. A través de los testamentos, la marca del discípulo es la misma: hay algo más valioso para él que su propia vida, y él sabe lo que es. El costo es nombrado de antemano, aceptado de antemano, y pagado a través de los años una obediencia a la vez.

blocks.en: 3. The Counterfeit
blocks.es_reference: 3. El Contrafactum

blocks.en: Matthew 16:26 (NKJV): "For what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?"
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 16:26 (RVG): "Porque ¿qué aprovechará al hombre, si ganare todo el mundo, y perdiere su alma? O ¿qué recompensa dará el hombre por su alma?"

blocks.en: The enemy of radical discipleship is not atheism. The enemy is materialism — the slow, cheerful substitution of things for the soul. Materialism is what makes the rich young ruler walk away from Jesus sorrowful, after asking the right question and receiving the right answer (Matt 19:22). It is what causes the seed of the word to be choked in Jesus' parable of the sower (Matt 13:22). It is what Charles Colson named when he wrote that we must first repent of idolatry, of having embraced the false gods of modern times, like materialism, power, success, and personal autonomy. Every standard the world uses to judge a man is the opposite of God's measure. To be great in the world, you must be powerful; to be great in the kingdom, you must be a servant. The world and the kingdom run on opposite currencies, and the disciple chooses which exchange rate his life will use.
blocks.es_reference: El enemigo del discipulado radical no es el ateísmo. El enemigo es el materialismo — la sustitución lenta y alegre de las cosas por el alma. El materialismo es lo que hace al joven rico irse de Jesús triste, después de hacer la pregunta correcta y recibir la respuesta correcta (Mat 19:22). Es lo que causa que la semilla de la palabra sea ahogada en la parábola del sembrador de Jesús (Mat 13:22). Es lo que Charles Colson nombró cuando escribió que debemos primero arrepentirnos de la idolatría, de haber abrazado los dioses falsos de los tiempos modernos, como el materialismo, el poder, el éxito, y la autonomía personal. Cada estándar que el mundo usa para juzgar a un hombre es el opuesto de la medida de Dios. Para ser grande en el mundo, debes ser poderoso; para ser grande en el reino, debes ser siervo. El mundo y el reino corren en monedas opuestas, y el discípulo escoge cuál tasa de cambio usará su vida.

blocks.en: The trouble is that materialism dresses up well. It usually does not look like greed. It looks like security, like responsibility, like being a good provider, like wanting the best for your children. It accumulates one defensible decision at a time until the wineskin is full of things that are not wine. Jesus' question in verse 26 is one of the sharpest in the Gospels: what will a man give in exchange for his soul? The honest answer in most lives is a long list of small things — none of them worth what they cost, all of them assembled into something that was. The disciple's first task is to refuse the trade before it is fully made.
blocks.es_reference: El problema es que el materialismo se viste bien. Usualmente no se ve como avaricia. Se ve como seguridad, como responsabilidad, como ser un buen proveedor, como querer lo mejor para tus hijos. Se acumula una decisión defendible a la vez hasta que el odre está lleno de cosas que no son vino. La pregunta de Jesús en el versículo 26 es una de las más agudas de los Evangelios: ¿qué recompensa dará el hombre por su alma? La respuesta honesta en la mayoría de las vidas es una larga lista de cosas pequeñas — ninguna de ellas valía lo que costó, todas ellas ensambladas en algo que sí lo valía. La primera tarea del discípulo es rechazar el intercambio antes de que esté completamente hecho.

blocks.en: The Russian Visitor: After many months of waiting, a Russian girl finally obtained a visa to visit her relatives in Canada for three months. She arrived and was shown all the attractions, the amusements, the entertainments. She was struck by how much things her hosts were wrapped up in. As her three months came to a close, everyone expected her to defect — to seek political asylum. She surprised them by going home. She explained that in North America everyone seemed wrapped up in things and had no time for people; in Russia they had fewer material possessions and therefore needed each other more. She wanted to return to a place where people relied on each other, where fellowship still mattered.
blocks.es_reference: La Visitante Rusa: Después de muchos meses de espera, una joven rusa finalmente obtuvo una visa para visitar a sus parientes en Canadá por tres meses. Llegó y le mostraron todas las atracciones, las diversiones, los entretenimientos. Le impresionó cuántas cosas envolvían a sus anfitriones. Cuando sus tres meses llegaron al cierre, todos esperaban que desertara — que buscara asilo político. Los sorprendió yéndose a casa. Explicó que en Norteamérica todos parecían envueltos en cosas y no tenían tiempo para personas; en Rusia tenían menos posesiones materiales y por eso se necesitaban más unos a otros. Quería regresar a un lugar donde la gente dependía unos de otros, donde la comunión aún importaba.

blocks.en: The Russian girl is not making a political argument; she is making a discipleship argument without using the word. She had been in a place where people had less and meant more to each other, and she had been in a place where people had more and meant less. Given the choice between the two, she chose less. The Lord's standard runs in the same direction. Materialism is not condemned because possessions are wicked but because possessions are heavy. They occupy space in the wineskin that was supposed to hold something else.
blocks.es_reference: La joven rusa no está haciendo un argumento político; está haciendo un argumento de discipulado sin usar la palabra. Había estado en un lugar donde la gente tenía menos y significaba más unos para otros, y había estado en un lugar donde la gente tenía más y significaba menos. Dada la elección entre los dos, escogió menos. El estándar del Señor corre en la misma dirección. El materialismo no es condenado porque las posesiones sean malvadas sino porque las posesiones son pesadas. Ocupan espacio en el odre que se suponía contendría otra cosa.

blocks.en: There is a counterfeit version of radical commitment in every age. In ours, it is often a political or social cause that demands the language of sacrifice while offering none of the soul-saving substance. The world has its own martyrs, its own missionaries, its own crusades. They are not the same thing as a disciple of Jesus. A radical without Christ is still serving an idol; the only difference is which one. Karl Marx is the obvious modern example — a deeply embittered man whose system promised the redemption of humanity through economics and produced graves in Russia, China, Cuba, and North Korea instead. He was radical. He was not a disciple. The cross he asked his followers to bear was someone else's, and the kingdom he promised never came. Jesus is more revolutionary than Marx; the difference is that joining His movement is voluntary, and the cross He asks His disciples to carry is the same one He carried first.
blocks.es_reference: Hay una versión falsificada del compromiso radical en cada edad. En la nuestra, frecuentemente es una causa política o social que demanda el lenguaje del sacrificio mientras no ofrece nada de la sustancia salvadora del alma. El mundo tiene sus propios mártires, sus propios misioneros, sus propias cruzadas. No son la misma cosa que un discípulo de Jesús. Un radical sin Cristo aún está sirviendo a un ídolo; la única diferencia es cuál. Karl Marx es el ejemplo moderno obvio — un hombre profundamente amargado cuyo sistema prometió la redención de la humanidad a través de la economía y produjo tumbas en Rusia, China, Cuba, y Corea del Norte en su lugar. Era radical. No era discípulo. La cruz que pidió a sus seguidores que llevaran era de otro, y el reino que prometió nunca vino. Jesús es más revolucionario que Marx; la diferencia es que unirse a Su movimiento es voluntario, y la cruz que pide a Sus discípulos cargar es la misma que Él cargó primero.

blocks.en: Radical discipleship is the new wineskin Jesus brought to replace religious rigidity. Its cost was named in advance: deny self, take up cross, follow. Its great enemy is materialism, the slow accumulation of things in the space the soul was meant to occupy. The Pharisees had old wineskins, the disciples had new ones, and Jesus walked between them looking for any container willing to stretch. The same Jesus still walks. The question every reader of Matthew 16 eventually has to answer is the question He asked the rich young ruler: what will you give in exchange for your soul? The disciple who has answered it once will keep answering it for the rest of his life, one obedience at a time.
blocks.es_reference: El discipulado radical es el odre nuevo que Jesús trajo para reemplazar la rigidez religiosa. Su costo fue nombrado de antemano: negarse a sí mismo, tomar la cruz, seguir. Su gran enemigo es el materialismo, la acumulación lenta de cosas en el espacio que el alma estaba destinada a ocupar. Los fariseos tenían odres viejos, los discípulos tenían nuevos, y Jesús caminó entre ellos buscando cualquier contenedor dispuesto a estirarse. El mismo Jesús aún camina. La pregunta que cada lector de Mateo 16 eventualmente tiene que responder es la pregunta que le hizo al joven rico: ¿qué darás a cambio de tu alma? El discípulo que la ha respondido una vez seguirá respondiéndola por el resto de su vida, una obediencia a la vez.

mc.why: Correct. Matthew 16:24 is the anchor verse for radical discipleship. Three commands stack inside one sentence: deny self, take up cross, follow. The unit unfolds the new wineskin Jesus brought, the cost He named, and the counterfeit the world keeps offering — but everything traces back to this single sentence.Correcto. Mateo 16:24 es el versículo ancla del discipulado radical. Tres mandamientos se apilan dentro de una oración: negarse a sí mismo, tomar la cruz, seguir. La unidad despliega el odre nuevo que Jesús trajo, el costo que Él nombró, y el contrafactum que el mundo sigue ofreciendo — pero todo se remonta a esta única oración.

D. Faith, hope, loveD. Fe, esperanza, amor
mc.why: Correct. The new wineskin (Matt 9:17), the cost (Matt 16:24-25), and the counterfeit (Matt 16:26, materialism). Each movement has its own scripture anchor and its own application. The wineskin is about flexibility; the cost is about price; the counterfeit is about the trade the world keeps offering instead of the real thing.Correcto. El odre nuevo (Mat 9:17), el costo (Mat 16:24-25), y el contrafactum (Mat 16:26, materialismo). Cada movimiento tiene su propia ancla de Escritura y su propia aplicación. El odre es sobre la flexibilidad; el costo es sobre el precio; el contrafactum es sobre el intercambio que el mundo sigue ofreciendo en vez de la cosa real.

mc.stem: 3. According to the unit, the wineskins image in Matthew 9:17 comes from:3. Según la unidad, la imagen de los odres en Mateo 9:17 viene de:
options: A. A vineyard at harvest timeA. Un viñedo en tiempo de cosecha
B. A Pharisee's debate over ceremonial lawB. Un debate de fariseos sobre la ley ceremonial
C. The kitchen, not a theology classroomC. La cocina, no un aula de teología
D. Ancient Roman trade routesD. Las rutas comerciales romanas antiguas
mc.why: Correct. Jesus drew His image from ordinary household life — fermentation, leather, gas pressure, a bag that has to stretch or split. The point is not about wine; the point is about people. The disciple He is making ferments; the disciple cannot be contained inside an old religious system that has no room left to stretch.Correcto. Jesús sacó Su imagen de la vida ordinaria del hogar — fermentación, cuero, presión de gas, una bolsa que tiene que estirarse o partirse. El punto no es sobre el vino; el punto es sobre las personas. El discípulo que Él está haciendo fermenta; el discípulo no puede ser contenido dentro de un viejo sistema religioso que no tiene espacio para estirarse.

mc.stem: 4. The two Pharisee complaints about Jesus that prompted the new-wineskins teaching (Matthew 9) were:4. Las dos quejas farisaicas sobre Jesús que provocaron la enseñanza de los odres nuevos (Mateo 9) fueron:
options: A. He worked on the Sabbath, and He taught in GreekA. Trabajaba en el sábado, y enseñaba en griego

B. He was eating with tax collectors and sinners, and His disciples were not fasting on the days the Pharisees fastedB. Estaba comiendo con recaudadores de impuestos y pecadores, y Sus discípulos no ayunaban en los días que los fariseos ayunaban
C. He called Himself the Son of Man, and He did not pay temple taxC. Se llamaba a Sí mismo el Hijo del Hombre, y no pagaba el impuesto del templo
D. He healed without a license, and He owned no propertyD. Sanaba sin licencia, y no poseía propiedad
mc.why: Correct. Both complaints were about containers. The Pharisees had a fixed shape for what a holy man should look like, and Jesus did not fit it. Rather than asking whether their shape might be wrong, they concluded He must be wrong. That is what an old wineskin does — it splits, blames the wine, and throws it away.Correcto. Ambas quejas eran sobre contenedores. Los fariseos tenían una forma fija de cómo debía verse un hombre santo, y Jesús no encajaba. En vez de preguntar si su forma podría estar equivocada, concluyeron que Él debía estar equivocado. Eso es lo que hace un odre viejo — se parte, culpa al vino, y lo tira.

mc.stem: 5. The most common kind of failure in church history, according to this unit, is:5. La clase de fracaso más común en la historia de la iglesia, según esta unidad, es:
options: A. Outright heresy and denial of ChristA. Herejía abierta y negación de Cristo
B. Not rigidity, but emotional excessB. No la rigidez, sino el exceso emocional
C. Failure to organize properlyC. Fallar en organizarse apropiadamente
D. Not heresy but rigidity, not denial but stiffnessD. No herejía sino rigidez, no negación sino tiesura
mc.why: Correct. Many believers reach the first stretch and decide they would rather have an unbroken old skin than a new one full of strange pressure. The wine spills. The skin is intact but empty. The Pharisees were not bad men by the world's standards — they were religious men whose containers could no longer hold what God was pouring.Correcto. Muchos creyentes alcanzan el primer estiramiento y deciden que prefieren tener un odre viejo intacto que uno nuevo lleno de presión extraña. El vino se derrama. El odre queda intacto pero vacío. Los fariseos no eran malos hombres según los estándares del mundo — eran hombres religiosos cuyos contenedores ya no podían sostener lo que Dios estaba vertiendo.

mc.stem: 6. In the Mrs. Brown illustration, what did the bubbles coming up through the water in the basin tell her about the wine?6. En la ilustración de la Sra. Brown, ¿qué le decían a ella las burbujas que subían a través del agua en la vasija sobre el vino?
options: A. Whether the wine was sweet enough yetA. Si el vino estaba lo bastante dulce todavía
B. When the bubbles stopped, the wine was finished — fermentation had completedB. Cuando las burbujas paraban, el vino estaba terminado — la fermentación había completado
C. The temperature of the liquidC. La temperatura del líquido
D. The color of the finished productD. El color del producto terminado
mc.why: Correct. The bubbles were CO₂ escaping through the water as the sugar in the juice fermented. When they stopped, the wine was done. That is what new wine does — it bubbles and ferments because the sugar in the juice is alive. A rigid container cannot hold that, and a disciple who has stopped fermenting in Christ is finished in a way Jesus did not intend.Correcto. Las burbujas eran CO₂ escapando a través del agua mientras el azúcar en el jugo fermentaba. Cuando paraban, el vino estaba listo. Eso es lo que hace el vino nuevo — burbujea y fermenta porque el azúcar en el jugo está vivo. Un contenedor rígido no puede contener eso, y un discípulo que ha dejado de fermentar en Cristo está terminado de una manera que Jesús no quiso.

mc.stem: 7. According to the unit, what did "take up his cross" mean to the Galilean crowd that first heard Matt 16:24?7. Según la unidad, ¿qué significaba "tome su cruz" para la multitud galilea que primero oyó Mat 16:24?
options: A. A devotional symbol they could wearA. Un símbolo devocional que podían llevar
B. The instrument of public, shameful execution — literal death and literal disgraceB. El instrumento de ejecución pública y vergonzosa — muerte literal y deshonra literal
C. A piece of architecture in the templeC. Una pieza de arquitectura en el templo
D. A heavy farming toolD. Una herramienta agrícola pesada
mc.why: Correct. A cross in the first century was not jewelry. Roman crucifixion was reserved for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals — public, shameful, slow. There was no devotional softness in the image. Jesus was naming the price of becoming His disciple, and the price was everything.Correcto. Una cruz en el primer siglo no era joyería. La crucifixión romana estaba reservada para esclavos, rebeldes, y los criminales más bajos — pública, vergonzosa, lenta. No había suavidad devocional en la imagen. Jesús estaba nombrando el precio de volverse Su discípulo, y el precio era todo.

mc.stem: 8. The unit notes that Jesus did not require of His disciples anything He had not done Himself. Which verse summarizes His own self-impoverishment for their sake?8. La unidad observa que Jesús no requirió de Sus discípulos nada que Él mismo no hubiera hecho. ¿Qué versículo resume Su propio empobrecimiento por amor a ellos?
options: A. Luke 9:51 — "He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem"A. Lucas 9:51 — "afirmó Su rostro para ir a Jerusalén"
B. John 1:14 — "the Word became flesh"B. Juan 1:14 — "el Verbo fue hecho carne"
C. 2 Corinthians 8:9 — "Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor"C. 2 Corintios 8:9 — "siendo rico, por amor de vosotros se hizo pobre"
D. Hebrews 4:15 — "tempted as we are, yet without sin"D. Hebreos 4:15 — "tentado en todo según nuestra semejanza, pero sin pecado"
mc.why: Correct. 2 Corinthians 8:9 — "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich." The Lord of glory left the throne. Every choice He made was a downward step. He did not ask His disciples to walk a road He had not already walked first.Correcto. 2 Corintios 8:9 — "siendo rico, por amor de vosotros se hizo pobre, para que vosotros con Su pobreza fueseis enriquecidos." El Señor de gloria dejó el trono. Cada decisión que tomó fue un paso hacia abajo. No pidió a Sus discípulos caminar un camino que Él mismo no hubiera caminado primero.

mc.stem: 9. According to the unit, Jesus had no grave of His own, but:9. Según la unidad, Jesús no tuvo tumba propia, sino que:
options: A. Had to borrow one when He died, though He did return it three days later, only slightly usedA. Tuvo que pedir prestada una cuando murió, aunque la devolvió tres días después, solo ligeramente usada
B. Was buried in a common pit with criminalsB. Fue enterrado en una fosa común con criminales
C. Was cremated according to Roman customC. Fue cremado según la costumbre romana
D. Disappeared from the cross without burialD. Desapareció de la cruz sin entierro
mc.why: Correct. Wayne's line is one of the unit's signatures: "He had no grave, but had to borrow one when He died — though He did return it three days later, only slightly used." The wit carries the doctrine. The Lord of glory owned nothing on earth, not even the hole He was buried in, and the empty tomb is the punchline of His self-impoverishment.Correcto. La línea de Wayne es una de las firmas de la unidad: "No tuvo tumba, pero tuvo que pedir prestada una cuando murió — aunque la devolvió tres días después, solo ligeramente usada." El ingenio carga la doctrina. El Señor de gloria no poseía nada en la tierra, ni siquiera el agujero en el que fue enterrado, y la tumba vacía es el remate de Su empobrecimiento.

mc.stem: 10. The verse Luke uses to mark the turning point in Jesus' ministry is:10. El versículo que Lucas usa para marcar el punto de giro en el ministerio de Jesús es:
options: A. Luke 9:51 — "He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem"A. Lucas 9:51 — "afirmó Su rostro para ir a Jerusalén"
B. Luke 2:7 — "she laid Him in a manger"B. Lucas 2:7 — "le acostó en un pesebre"
C. Luke 4:18 — "the Spirit of the Lord is upon Me"C. Lucas 4:18 — "el Espíritu del Señor es sobre Mí"
D. Luke 22:42 — "not My will, but Yours, be done"D. Lucas 22:42 — "no se haga Mi voluntad, sino la tuya"
mc.why: Correct. Luke 9:51. Jesus knew what was waiting in Jerusalem — the cross was visible from the moment He turned His face toward it. He went anyway. The disciple's pattern is the same: name the cost in advance, accept it in advance, walk toward it without flinching when the road bends downward.Correcto. Lucas 9:51. Jesús sabía lo que esperaba en Jerusalén — la cruz era visible desde el momento que afirmó Su rostro hacia ella. Fue de todos modos. El patrón del discípulo es el mismo: nombrar el costo de antemano, aceptarlo de antemano, caminar hacia él sin estremecerse cuando el camino se inclina hacia abajo.

mc.stem: 11. According to the unit, what eventually happened to most of the apostles?11. Según la unidad, ¿qué le pasó eventualmente a la mayoría de los apóstoles?
options: A. They retired peacefully in their hometownsA. Se retiraron pacíficamente en sus ciudades natales
B. They were absorbed into the Roman administrationB. Fueron absorbidos en la administración romana
C. They returned to their original tradesC. Regresaron a sus oficios originales

D. By the end of the first century, most of them had sacrificed their lives — only John lived to old age, in exile on PatmosD. Para el final del primer siglo, la mayoría había sacrificado sus vidas — solo Juan vivió hasta la vejez, en exilio en Patmos
mc.why: Correct. James was beheaded (Acts 12:2); well-attested church tradition holds Peter was crucified and Andrew and Thomas died as martyrs too, Thomas as far as India; only John lived to old age, and he lived it in exile. The standard for radical commitment did not change between Jesus and the apostles — "whoever wants to come after Me" still means deny self, take up cross, follow. The apostles paid the full price slowly across the decades.Correcto. Jacobo fue decapitado (Hechos 12:2); la tradición bien atestiguada de la iglesia sostiene que Pedro fue crucificado y que Andrés y Tomás también murieron como mártires, Tomás tan lejos como India; solo Juan vivió hasta la vejez, y la vivió en exilio. El estándar para el compromiso radical no cambió entre Jesús y los apóstoles — "si alguno quiere venir en pos de Mí" aún significa negarse a sí mismo, tomar la cruz, seguir. Los apóstoles pagaron el precio completo lentamente a través de las décadas.

mc.stem: 12. Acts 5:29, quoted by Peter before the Sanhedrin, expresses what radical-discipleship principle?12. Hechos 5:29, citado por Pedro ante el Sanedrín, expresa qué principio de discipulado radical?
options: A. "We ought to obey God rather than men"A. "Es necesario obedecer a Dios antes que a los hombres"
B. "Greater works than these shall you do"B. "Mayores obras que éstas haréis"
C. "By their fruits you will know them"C. "Por sus frutos los conoceréis"
D. "The just shall live by faith"D. "El justo vivirá por fe"
mc.why: Correct. "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29). Peter said it knowing exactly what the consequences would be. Across the testaments, the disciple's mark is the same: there is something more valuable to him than his own life, and he knows what it is. The cost is named in advance, accepted in advance, paid out one obedience at a time.Correcto. "Es necesario obedecer a Dios antes que a los hombres" (Hch 5:29). Pedro lo dijo sabiendo exactamente cuáles serían las consecuencias. A través de los testamentos, la marca del discípulo es la misma: hay algo más valioso para él que su propia vida, y él sabe lo que es. El costo es nombrado de antemano, aceptado de antemano, pagado una obediencia a la vez.

mc.stem: 13. The unit names the enemy of radical discipleship. It is NOT atheism. It is:13. La unidad nombra al enemigo del discipulado radical. NO es el ateísmo. Es:
options: A. Political persecutionA. La persecución política
B. False teachingB. La enseñanza falsa
C. Materialism — the slow, cheerful substitution of things for the soulC. El materialismo — la sustitución lenta y alegre de las cosas por el alma
D. Theological controversyD. La controversia teológica
mc.why: Correct. Materialism. It is what makes the rich young ruler walk away sorrowful after asking the right question and receiving the right answer. It chokes the seed of the word in the parable of the sower. It usually does not look like greed — it looks like security, responsibility, being a good provider, wanting the best for your children. It accumulates one defensible decision at a time until the wineskin is full of things that are not wine.Correcto. El materialismo. Es lo que hace al joven rico irse triste después de hacer la pregunta correcta y recibir la respuesta correcta. Ahoga la semilla de la palabra en la parábola del sembrador. Usualmente no se ve como avaricia — se ve como seguridad, responsabilidad, ser un buen proveedor, querer lo mejor para tus hijos. Se acumula una decisión defendible a la vez hasta que el odre está lleno de cosas que no son vino.

mc.stem: 14. Charles Colson, quoted in the unit, names what the modern church must first repent of:14. Charles Colson, citado en la unidad, nombra de qué debe arrepentirse primero la iglesia moderna:
options: A. Bad music in worshipA. Mala música en la adoración

B. Idolatry — embracing false gods of modern times: materialism, power, success, personal autonomyB. La idolatría — abrazar a los dioses falsos de los tiempos modernos: materialismo, poder, éxito, autonomía personal
C. Lack of evangelistic enthusiasmC. Falta de entusiasmo evangelístico
D. Doctrinal disagreements between denominationsD. Desacuerdos doctrinales entre denominaciones
mc.why: Correct. Colson named four modern idols by name: materialism, power, success, personal autonomy. Every standard the world uses to judge a man is the opposite of God's measure. To be great in the world, you must be powerful; to be great in the kingdom, you must be a servant. The world and the kingdom run on opposite currencies, and the disciple chooses which exchange rate his life will use.Correcto. Colson nombró cuatro ídolos modernos por nombre: materialismo, poder, éxito, autonomía personal. Cada estándar que el mundo usa para juzgar a un hombre es el opuesto de la medida de Dios. Para ser grande en el mundo, debes ser poderoso; para ser grande en el reino, debes ser siervo. El mundo y el reino corren en monedas opuestas, y el discípulo escoge cuál tasa de cambio usará su vida.

mc.stem: 15. The Russian girl who visited her relatives in Canada surprised them by:15. La joven rusa que visitó a sus parientes en Canadá los sorprendió:
options: A. Seeking political asylum and defectingA. Buscando asilo político y desertando
B. Marrying a Canadian and staying permanentlyB. Casándose con un canadiense y quedándose permanentemente
C. Refusing to leave her hotelC. Rehusándose a salir de su hotel

D. Returning to Russia, explaining that North Americans were wrapped up in things and had no time for peopleD. Regresando a Rusia, explicando que los norteamericanos estaban envueltos en cosas y no tenían tiempo para las personas
mc.why: Correct. She had been in a place where people had less and meant more to each other, and a place where people had more and meant less. Given the choice between the two, she chose less. The Lord's standard runs in the same direction: materialism is not condemned because possessions are wicked but because possessions are heavy. They occupy space in the wineskin that was supposed to hold something else.Correcto. Había estado en un lugar donde la gente tenía menos y significaba más unos para otros, y un lugar donde la gente tenía más y significaba menos. Dada la elección entre los dos, escogió menos. El estándar del Señor corre en la misma dirección: el materialismo no es condenado porque las posesiones sean malvadas sino porque las posesiones son pesadas. Ocupan espacio en el odre que se suponía contendría otra cosa.

mc.stem: 16. According to the unit, the disciple's first task regarding materialism is to:16. Según la unidad, la primera tarea del discípulo respecto al materialismo es:
options: A. Sell all possessions immediatelyA. Vender todas las posesiones inmediatamente
B. Take a vow of poverty for lifeB. Tomar un voto de pobreza de por vida
C. Avoid all commerce and bankingC. Evitar todo comercio y banca
D. Refuse the trade before it is fully madeD. Rechazar el intercambio antes de que esté completamente hecho
mc.why: Correct. Materialism accumulates one defensible decision at a time until the soul has been traded away in small pieces. The honest answer to "what will a man give in exchange for his soul?" is, in most lives, a long list of small things — none of them worth what they cost, all of them assembled into something that was. The disciple refuses the trade early, before it is too late to notice it.Correcto. El materialismo se acumula una decisión defendible a la vez hasta que el alma ha sido intercambiada en pequeñas piezas. La respuesta honesta a "¿qué dará un hombre a cambio de su alma?" es, en la mayoría de las vidas, una larga lista de cosas pequeñas — ninguna de ellas valía lo que costó, todas ellas ensambladas en algo que sí. El discípulo rechaza el intercambio temprano, antes de que sea demasiado tarde para notarlo.

mc.stem: 17. The unit gives Karl Marx as a modern example of:17. La unidad da a Karl Marx como un ejemplo moderno de:
options: A. A radical who was also a Christian discipleA. Un radical que también era un discípulo cristiano
B. A theologian whose work was misunderstoodB. Un teólogo cuya obra fue malentendida

C. A radical without Christ — a counterfeit version of radical commitment, serving an idol rather than the LordC. Un radical sin Cristo — una versión falsificada del compromiso radical, sirviendo a un ídolo en vez del Señor
D. A monk who broke his vowsD. Un monje que rompió sus votos
mc.why: Correct. A radical without Christ is still serving an idol; the only difference is which one. Marx was deeply embittered, and his system promised the redemption of humanity through economics but produced graves in Russia, China, Cuba, and North Korea. He was radical. He was not a disciple. The cross he asked his followers to bear was someone else's, and the kingdom he promised never came.Correcto. Un radical sin Cristo aún está sirviendo a un ídolo; la única diferencia es cuál. Marx estaba profundamente amargado, y su sistema prometió la redención de la humanidad a través de la economía pero produjo tumbas en Rusia, China, Cuba, y Corea del Norte. Era radical. No era discípulo. La cruz que pidió a sus seguidores que llevaran era de otro, y el reino que prometió nunca vino.

mc.stem: 18. The unit says the key difference between Jesus' movement and Marx's is:18. La unidad dice que la diferencia clave entre el movimiento de Jesús y el de Marx es:
options: A. The historical periodA. El período histórico
B. The language each usedB. El idioma que cada uno usó
C. The number of followers each attractedC. El número de seguidores que cada uno atrajo

D. Joining Jesus' movement is voluntary, and the cross He asks His disciples to carry is the same one He carried firstD. Unirse al movimiento de Jesús es voluntario, y la cruz que pide a Sus discípulos cargar es la misma que Él cargó primero
mc.why: Correct. Voluntary participation; shared cross. Marx's revolutions were imposed and produced compulsion. Jesus' revolution is offered and produces willing surrender. The leaders of forced revolutions ride at the head of armies; the Leader of this one rode at the head of a procession to His own execution. The disciples follow not because they were drafted but because they were invited.Correcto. Participación voluntaria; cruz compartida. Las revoluciones de Marx fueron impuestas y produjeron compulsión. La revolución de Jesús es ofrecida y produce rendición voluntaria. Los líderes de las revoluciones forzadas cabalgan a la cabeza de los ejércitos; el Líder de ésta cabalgó a la cabeza de una procesión a Su propia ejecución. Los discípulos siguen no porque fueran reclutados sino porque fueron invitados.

mc.stem: 19. The unit's summary describes the three components of radical discipleship as:19. El resumen de la unidad describe los tres componentes del discipulado radical como:
options: A. New wineskin (replacing rigidity), named cost (deny self, take cross, follow), and great enemy (materialism)A. Odre nuevo (reemplazando rigidez), costo nombrado (negarse, tomar cruz, seguir), y gran enemigo (materialismo)
B. Conversion, baptism, communionB. Conversión, bautismo, comunión
C. Belief, behavior, belongingC. Creencia, conducta, pertenencia
D. Past, present, futureD. Pasado, presente, futuro
mc.why: Correct. New wineskin, named cost, great enemy. The Pharisees had old wineskins; the disciples had new ones; and Jesus walked between them looking for any container willing to stretch. The same Jesus still walks. The question every reader of Matthew 16 eventually has to answer is the question He asked the rich young ruler: what will you give in exchange for your soul?Correcto. Odre nuevo, costo nombrado, gran enemigo. Los fariseos tenían odres viejos; los discípulos tenían nuevos; y Jesús caminó entre ellos buscando cualquier contenedor dispuesto a estirarse. El mismo Jesús aún camina. La pregunta que cada lector de Mateo 16 eventualmente tiene que responder es la pregunta que le hizo al joven rico: ¿qué darás a cambio de tu alma?

mc.stem: 20. The closing application question of the unit, asked of every reader, is essentially the question Jesus asked the rich young ruler:20. La pregunta de aplicación de cierre de la unidad, hecha a cada lector, es esencialmente la pregunta que Jesús le hizo al joven rico:
options: A. Do you tithe a full ten percent?A. ¿Diezmas el diez por ciento completo?
B. Have you been baptized properly?B. ¿Has sido bautizado apropiadamente?
C. What will you give in exchange for your soul?C. ¿Qué darás a cambio de tu alma?
D. Are you attending church regularly?D. ¿Estás asistiendo a la iglesia regularmente?
mc.why: Correct. "What will you give in exchange for your soul?" The disciple who has answered it once will keep answering it for the rest of his life, one obedience at a time. The question is not asked once at conversion; it is asked every time materialism offers another small trade. The early no is the only no that works, and the disciple practices saying it across decades.Correcto. "¿Qué darás a cambio de tu alma?" El discípulo que la ha respondido una vez seguirá respondiéndola por el resto de su vida, una obediencia a la vez. La pregunta no se hace una vez en la conversión; se hace cada vez que el materialismo ofrece otro pequeño intercambio. El no temprano es el único no que funciona, y el discípulo practica decirlo a través de las décadas.

sa.prompt: Explain why Jesus' wineskins image (Matthew 9:16-17) is fundamentally about people, not about wine. Use the chemistry of fermentation in your answer.
sa.model: New wine ferments — the sugar in the juice becomes gas, the gas expands, the container has to stretch. A fresh leather wineskin gives a little as the wine breathes, then more, then settles when fermentation finishes. An old, brittle wineskin has no give; the same pressure that a new skin absorbs splits an old one open. Jesus' point is about people: the disciple He is making is fermenting, alive, expansive. The disciple cannot be contained inside an old religious system that has no room left to stretch. The Pharisees were rigid containers; what Jesus was pouring into them split them open. Faith in Christ is not ordinary but revolutionary — and revolutionary faith requires a wineskin that can stretch without breaking.

sa.prompt: Tell the Mrs. Brown milk-jugs story and explain what Wayne uses it to teach about the nature of new wine and the nature of living faith.
sa.model: When Wayne was a teenager, his mother hired Mrs. Brown to do the ironing, and Wayne's job was to deliver and pick up the clothes. Mrs. Brown had milk jugs filled with colored liquid, with tubes leading down to a basin of water. When Wayne asked, she explained it was wine inside; when the bubbles stopped coming up through the water, the wine was finished. Wayne uses this small kitchen detail to teach a serious doctrine. New wine bubbles because the sugar in the juice is alive — fermentation is a sign of life. Living faith behaves the same way: it is expansive, it stretches its container, it does not sit politely inside whatever religious shape the disciple grew up in. A rigid container cannot hold living wine; a still faith is a finished faith. The disciple who is no longer being stretched has settled into an old wineskin and is, in Wayne's framing, finished in a way Jesus did not intend.

sa.prompt: Walk through Matthew 16:24 phrase by phrase. What does 'deny himself' mean, what did 'take up his cross' mean to a first-century audience, and what makes 'follow Me' an ongoing rather than one-time command?
sa.model: Deny himself names the self as the largest obstacle to discipleship — not external enemies, not circumstances, but the person inside the disciple who wants to save his own life. Take up his cross meant something brutal in the first century. A cross was the instrument of public, shameful execution reserved for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals. There was no devotional softness in the image; when Jesus said it to a Galilean crowd, they heard 'be ready to die a slave's death for Me.' Follow Me is the ongoing verb. The denial and the cross-taking are not one-time moments; they are repeated as long as the disciple keeps following. The cost is named in advance, accepted in advance, and paid out across the years one obedience at a time.

sa.prompt: Catalogue the ways Jesus' own life demonstrated radical commitment, as the unit describes them. Include 2 Corinthians 8:9, His material poverty, His borrowed possessions, and Luke 9:51.
sa.model: Jesus did not ask of His disciples anything He had not done. 2 Cor 8:9: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor.' He left the throne of glory. He took a body, took a stable for His birthplace and a manger for His crib. He had no house during His ministry and no savings — only a nice cloak someone had given Him. He had no horse and had to borrow a colt for His final entrance into Jerusalem. He had no grave but had to borrow one when He died, though He did return it three days later only slightly used. Every choice was a downward step. Luke 9:51 marks the turning point: 'He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem.' He knew what was waiting there — the cross was visible from the moment He turned His face toward it. He went anyway. The disciple's standard is therefore not theoretical; it is the actual life the master lived.

sa.prompt: Trace the apostles' progressive cost from their first call to their final days. What did they sacrifice at the start, in the middle, and at the end?
sa.model: The apostles paid the cost progressively. At the start they sacrificed their jobs — fishing nets dropped on the beach, a tax-collector's table abandoned mid-collection. In the middle they sacrificed their reputations, walking publicly with a teacher the religious authorities openly hated. At the end, most of them sacrificed their lives. James was beheaded (Acts 12:2); church tradition, well-attested though not itself Scripture, holds that Peter was crucified and Andrew and Thomas died as martyrs as well, Thomas as far away as India; only John lived to old age, and he lived it in exile on Patmos. The standard for radical commitment did not change between Jesus and the apostles. 'Whoever wants to come after Me' still meant deny self, take up cross, follow. The cost named in Matthew 16:24 was paid out one obedience at a time until each man's last obedience was his last breath.

sa.prompt: Explain why the unit says the enemy of radical discipleship is materialism rather than atheism. How does materialism work — what does it usually look like, and why is it harder to recognize than open denial?
sa.model: Atheism announces itself loudly; materialism slips in quietly. Materialism is the slow, cheerful substitution of things for the soul. It usually does not look like greed. It looks like security, like responsibility, like being a good provider, like wanting the best for your children. Every individual purchase is defensible. The accumulation is not. One defensible decision at a time fills the wineskin with things that are not wine, until the soul has been traded away in small pieces no one ever named as opposition. Atheism is something a disciple can prepare to resist because it announces itself; materialism arrives wearing the disciple's own values. The disciple who has steeled himself against denial of Christ may still lose ground daily to small accumulations he does not see as enemy action.

sa.prompt: Quote and explain Matthew 16:26 in your own words. Why does the unit call this question 'one of the sharpest in the Gospels,' and what is the honest answer in most lives?
sa.model: Matthew 16:26: 'What profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?' The question is sharp because the math is sharp: there is no asset gained in the world worth the cost of the soul that buys it. The unit calls it one of the sharpest because it punctures every rationalization at once — no asset, no relationship, no career, no inheritance, no comfort, no security can be priced high enough to cover the loss it asks. The honest answer in most lives is a long list of small things, none of them worth what they cost, all of them assembled into something that was. That is how materialism works: small trades, defensible one at a time, devastating in total. The disciple's first task is to refuse the trade before it is fully made.

sa.prompt: Tell the Russian visitor story and explain why the unit treats her decision as a discipleship argument rather than a political one.
sa.model: After many months of waiting, a Russian girl obtained a visa to visit her relatives in Canada for three months. She was shown the attractions, amusements, entertainments. She was struck by how much things her hosts were wrapped up in. As her three months closed, everyone expected her to seek political asylum. She surprised them by going home, explaining that in North America everyone seemed wrapped up in things and had no time for people; in Russia they had fewer possessions and needed each other more, and she wanted to return to a place where fellowship still mattered. The unit treats this as a discipleship argument rather than a political one because she was not arguing communism vs. capitalism; she was arguing that materialism crowds out community, and community is what people are made for. Less stuff, more people. The Lord's standard runs in the same direction — materialism is not condemned because possessions are wicked but because possessions are heavy. They occupy space in the wineskin that was supposed to hold something else.

sa.prompt: Why does the unit use Karl Marx as the counterfeit of radical commitment? What did he produce, why was he radical, and what specifically made him not a disciple?
sa.model: Marx is the unit's example of a radical without Christ — still serving an idol, just a different one. He was deeply embittered, and his system promised the redemption of humanity through economics but produced graves in Russia, China, Cuba, and North Korea instead. He was radical: he demanded everything from his followers, he wrote with the certainty of a prophet, he gave his life to his cause. He was not a disciple: he served an idol called History, the cross he asked his followers to bear was not his (he wrote in a library while others bled in factories and prisons), and the kingdom he promised never came. The unit's contrast is sharp: Jesus is more revolutionary than Marx, but joining His movement is voluntary, and the cross He asks His disciples to carry is the same one He carried first. Marx demands without giving; Jesus invites after having gone first. Both produce radicals; only one produces disciples.

sa.prompt: Synthesize the unit's three movements (new wineskin, named cost, great enemy) and explain how the closing question — 'What will you give in exchange for your soul?' — is answered not once but throughout a disciple's whole life.
sa.model: Radical discipleship is the new wineskin Jesus brought to replace religious rigidity — the new container that can stretch to hold what He is pouring. The cost was named in advance and is unchanged: deny self, take up cross, follow. The great enemy is materialism — not atheism, not persecution, but the slow accumulation of things in the space the soul was meant to occupy. The Pharisees had old wineskins; the disciples had new ones; Jesus walked between them looking for any container willing to stretch. The same Jesus still walks. The closing question — 'What will you give in exchange for your soul?' — is the question He asked the rich young ruler, and it is the question He keeps asking. The disciple who has answered it once will keep answering it for the rest of his life, one obedience at a time, because materialism keeps offering the next small trade. The cost is paid not in a single dramatic moment but in the daily refusal to sell the soul piece by piece. Radical discipleship is therefore not a graduation but a lifelong posture.
